title: Magnetic field around a circular coil
question: A circular coil carries current anticlockwise when viewed from the front. Which statement describes its magnetic polarity and the effect of reversing the current?

options.text: The front face is South, and reversing current leaves its polarity unchanged.
The front face is North, and reversing current makes the front face South.
The front face is North, and reversing current makes both faces North.
The front face has no magnetic polarity because the conductor is circular.

explanation: By the clock rule, anticlockwise current makes the viewed face North. Reversing the current makes it clockwise, so that face becomes South.

title: A conductor moved through a magnetic field
question: A straight conductor is moved through a magnetic field so that it cuts magnetic field lines. Its motion is then changed to be parallel to the magnetic field lines. What happens to the induced emf, assuming the other conditions are unchanged?

options.text: It doubles because the conductor moves along the field.
It remains the same because the magnetic field strength is unchanged.
It becomes zero because the conductor no longer cuts across the field lines.
It reverses direction but retains the same magnitude.

explanation: In the second arrangement, the conductor moves parallel to the field lines and does not cut across them. The motional induction described in this situation therefore becomes zero.

options.text: The secondary has an induced emf, but its load current is zero because the secondary circuit is open.
The secondary has zero voltage because no current flows in it.
The primary current must be zero because the secondary circuit is open.
The transformer produces DC at the secondary terminals.

explanation: The alternating magnetic flux induces a secondary emf even when the secondary is open. With no closed secondary path, no load current flows. In an ideal model, the primary draws no current under a perfect open-secondary, no-loss assumption except as needed for idealisation; real transformers draw magnetising current.

title: Electromagnet strength: Turns and current
question: Two otherwise identical solenoids have the same core and length. Solenoid P has 200 turns carrying 1 A. Solenoid Q has 400 turns carrying 0.5 A. Using the school-level approximation that field strength depends on turns per unit length multiplied by current, which conclusion is best?

options.text: P must be twice as strong as Q.
Q must be twice as strong as P.
Neither produces a magnetic field because their currents differ.
Their magnetic field strengths are approximately equal under the stated assumptions.

explanation:
The products of turns and current are equal:


200×1=400×0.5


For the same length and core, the approximate magnetising effect is therefore the same.

title: Motor and generator: Reversing rotation
question: A simple AC generator produces an emf while its coil rotates clockwise. The coil is then driven anticlockwise at the same speed, with the same magnetic field and connections. What happens to the generated emf at corresponding coil positions?

options.text: Its frequency becomes zero.
Its polarity sequence reverses, while the frequency and maximum magnitude remain the same under ideal conditions.
Its maximum magnitude becomes twice as large.
The output becomes steady DC.

explanation: Reversing the direction of rotation reverses the direction in which the coil cuts the field, so the induced emf polarity sequence reverses. Equal speed and unchanged field and coil give the same frequency and maximum magnitude.

title: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
question: Why does the induced current in a coil oppose the change in magnetic flux that produces it?

options.text: To increase the magnetic flux without requiring external work.
Because induced current always flows clockwise, regardless of the magnet's motion.
To oppose the change, consistent with conservation of energy; external work may be required to move the magnet.
Because a coil cannot produce a magnetic field of its own.

explanation: Lenz's law gives the direction of the induced current. Its opposing effect prevents energy from being generated without work. For example, pushing a magnet into a coil requires work against the induced magnetic repulsion.

title: A transformer with an altered supply frequency
question: An ideal transformer is operated at the same RMS primary voltage but at a lower AC frequency. Which statement is the most appropriate?

options.text: The maximum core flux tends to increase, since flux is inversely related to frequency at fixed voltage and turns.
The secondary voltage must become zero because the supply is AC.
The core flux must remain unchanged at every frequency.
The transformer automatically converts the supply into DC.

explanation: For a sinusoidal supply, the induced voltage is proportional to frequency, turns and maximum flux. At fixed voltage and turns, lowering the frequency tends to increase maximum flux, potentially causing core saturation and excessive current.

title: Comparing AC and DC generator output
question: A simple DC generator and a simple AC generator have identical coils, magnetic fields and rotational speeds. Their commutator arrangements differ. Which statement best distinguishes their outputs?

options.text: Both always produce perfectly constant voltage.
The AC generator uses a split-ring commutator to reverse the field.
The DC generator produces alternating current because its brushes are stationary.
The AC generator uses slip rings for alternating output; the DC generator uses a split-ring commutator for unidirectional, pulsating output.

explanation: Slip rings preserve the alternating output of the rotating coil. A split-ring commutator reverses the coil's connections every half-turn, making the external output unidirectional, though not perfectly steady.

title: A multi-step transformer application
question: An ideal transformer operates at 230 V on its primary and delivers 23 V on its secondary. The primary current is 0.4 A. Which pair gives the secondary current and the transformer type?

options.text: 0.04 A, step-up.
4 A, step-down.
0.4 A, step-down.
4 A, step-up.

explanation:
The voltage ratio is 23/230=1/10, so it is step-down. For an ideal transformer:


V_pI_p=V_sI_s



I_s=(230×0.4 / 23)=4 A

title: Integrated concept: Motor, induction and energy
question: A student rotates the shaft of an unpowered DC motor by hand while its terminals are connected to a galvanometer. A brief deflection is observed. Which explanation best accounts for this result?

options.text: The motor draws electrical energy from the battery even though none is connected.
The permanent magnets lose all their magnetism when the shaft moves.
The rotating armature changes its magnetic flux linkage, producing an induced emf and a current through the galvanometer circuit.
Mechanical rotation produces charge from nothing, independently of magnetic fields.

explanation:
best accounts for this result?

A) The motor draws electrical energy from the battery even though none is connected.

B) The permanent magnets lose all their magnetism when the shaft moves.

C) The rotating armature changes its magnetic flux linkage, producing an induced emf and a current through the galvanometer circuit.

D) Mechanical rotation produces charge from nothing, independently of magnetic fields.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** When the armature rotates in the magnetic field, its flux linkage changes and an emf is induced. If the circuit is complete, a current flows. This is the generator effect operating in a machine originally designed as a motor.

title: Magnetic field and force: Two independent reversals
question: A horizontal conductor carries conventional current from west to east. It is placed in a magnetic field directed vertically downward. The conductor experiences a force. The current is then reversed, and subsequently the magnetic field is also reversed. What is the final force direction compared with the original force?

options.text: Opposite to the original direction.
Vertically upward.
The same as the original direction.
Zero, because both directions have been reversed.

explanation: Reversing either current or magnetic field alone reverses the force. Reversing both restores the original force direction, assuming the magnitudes and conductor orientation are unchanged.

title: Solenoid polarity and induced current
question: A North pole of a bar magnet approaches the left end of a coil. The coil is connected to a galvanometer. The magnet is then withdrawn along the same axis. Which statement correctly describes the coil's response?

options.text: The left face is North during approach and South during withdrawal; the induced current reverses.
The left face is South during approach and North during withdrawal; the induced current remains unchanged.
The left face remains North during both motions because the same magnet pole is involved.
No induced current occurs because the magnet does not touch the coil.

explanation: By Lenz's law, the coil opposes the change causing induction. It repels the approaching North pole and attracts the receding North pole. The induced current therefore reverses when the direction of motion reverses.

title: Transformer and transmission loss
question: An ideal transformer raises a supply voltage from 240 V to 2400 V for transmitting a fixed power through a resistive line. Compared with transmitting at 240 V, what happens to the line current and the power loss?

options.text: Current becomes ten times greater; loss becomes one hundred times greater.
Current becomes one-tenth; loss becomes one-hundredth.
Current becomes one-tenth; loss becomes one-tenth.
Current remains unchanged; loss becomes one-hundredth.

explanation: For fixed power, P=VI, so increasing voltage tenfold reduces current to one-tenth. Since line loss is I^2R, the loss becomes (1/10)²=1/100, provided line resistance is unchanged.

title: Motor commutator and torque
question: A student removes the split-ring commutator from a simple DC motor but leaves the brushes, coil, field magnet and DC supply unchanged. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: The motor continues rotating indefinitely in the same direction with unchanged torque.
The magnetic field of the permanent magnet reverses every half-turn.
The motor becomes an AC generator without any mechanical input.
The coil's current no longer reverses every half-turn, so the torque tends to reverse and continuous rotation is not maintained reliably.

explanation: The commutator reverses the armature current every half-turn. Without this reversal, the torque changes sense as the coil rotates, preventing sustained rotation in the intended direction.

title: Generator speed and induced emf
question: A simple AC generator is operated at twice its original rotational speed, with the same coil and magnetic field. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its frequency doubles, and its maximum induced emf generally doubles.
Its frequency remains unchanged, but its maximum emf doubles.
Its frequency doubles, but its maximum emf must become zero.
Both frequency and maximum emf remain unchanged.

explanation: Faster rotation makes the flux linkage change more rapidly, increasing the maximum induced emf. It also produces more cycles per second, so the frequency doubles under otherwise unchanged conditions.

title: Transformer turns and current
question: An ideal transformer has 1,200 turns in its primary and 300 turns in its secondary. Its primary is connected to a 240 V AC supply and draws 2 A. Which pair gives the secondary voltage and secondary current when a load is connected?
explanation:
V_s=240≤ft((300 / 1200)right)=60 V


For an ideal transformer,


V_pI_p=V_sI_s



I_s=(240×2 / 60)=8 A


It is a step-down transformer, so the secondary current is greater than the primary current.

title: Electromagnet: Separating strength from polarity
question: A solenoid's current is doubled and then reversed. Assume the core remains in its normal operating range and all other conditions are unchanged. Which description is best?

options.text: Its polarity remains unchanged and its strength halves.
Its polarity reverses and its strength becomes zero.
Its polarity reverses, and its magnetic field is generally stronger than before the current was doubled.
Its polarity reverses, but the field must be exactly four times as strong.

explanation: Reversing current reverses the magnetic polarity. Increasing the current generally increases the field strength. The exact factor is not guaranteed to be four; that would not follow from doubling current.

title: Electromagnetic induction: Separating speed and turns
question: Two coils are exposed to the same changing magnetic field. Coil P has 100 turns, and coil Q has 200 turns. Assume the flux change per turn is identical and occurs over the same time interval. What is the relationship between the magnitudes of their induced emfs?

options.text: Coil P has twice the emf of coil Q.
Both have the same emf because the magnetic field is the same.
Coil Q has four times the emf of coil P.
Coil Q has twice the emf of coil P.

explanation: The induced emf is proportional to the number of turns for the same change in flux per turn over the same time. Doubling the turns doubles the induced emf.

title: Identifying the machine from its output
question: A rotating coil produces an alternating emf. The coil ends connect to two continuous slip rings, which touch stationary brushes. Which device is being described?

options.text: A simple AC generator.
A simple DC motor.
A transformer.
An electric bell.

explanation: An AC generator uses slip rings to connect the rotating coil to the external circuit. A simple DC generator uses a split-ring commutator to make the external output unidirectional.

title: Transformer losses and core design
question: A transformer has excessive heating in its iron core. Which change directly addresses eddy-current loss without confusing it with copper loss?

options.text: Replace the insulated laminations with one thick solid iron block.
Use a laminated core made of thin, electrically insulated sheets.
Increase the resistance of the primary winding.
Increase the secondary load current deliberately.

explanation: Thin insulated laminations restrict circulating eddy currents in the core. Copper loss occurs in the windings and is reduced by lowering their resistance, not by increasing it.

title: Current direction, field direction and force
question: A straight conductor carries current vertically upward. The magnetic field is directed horizontally from north to south. Which method should be used to determine the force direction, and why?

options.text: The right-hand thumb rule, because it determines force directly.
The clock rule, because it identifies the conductor's magnetic poles.
Fleming's left-hand rule, because it relates magnetic field, conventional current and force.
Fleming's right-hand rule, because current is being supplied by a battery.

explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule is used for the motor effect. The right-hand thumb rule determines the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor, while Fleming's right-hand rule is used for induced current in the generator effect.

title: AC generator at a particular coil position
question: In a simple AC generator, the coil rotates uniformly in a uniform magnetic field. At one instant, the flux linkage through the coil is zero. Which statement is correct for the idealised rotating-coil model?

options.text: The induced emf must be zero because the flux is zero.
The induced emf is generally at its maximum magnitude because the flux linkage is changing most rapidly.
The induced emf must be constant for the next half-turn.
The generator has stopped producing emf because there is no flux through the coil.

explanation: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage, not on flux alone. In the idealised model, when flux linkage passes through zero, its rate of change is greatest, so the induced emf has maximum magnitude.

title: Comparing two transmission systems
question: Two systems transmit the same electrical power through wires of equal resistance. System P operates at 500 V, while system Q operates at 2000 V. Assume ideal voltage conversion and identical power factors for this comparison. What is the ratio of their resistive line losses, P_P:P_Q?
explanation: For equal power, current is inversely proportional to voltage. System Q uses four times the voltage, so its current is one-quarter of P's. As line loss is proportional to current squared, P_P:P_Q=1:(1/4)²=16:1.

title: Why an electric bell vibrates repeatedly
question: An electric bell continues ringing while its switch is held on. Which sequence best explains the repeated motion?

options.text: The electromagnet attracts the armature; the contact breaks; current stops; magnetism weakens; the spring restores contact; the cycle repeats.
The electromagnet remains permanently magnetised and pushes the armature away without contact changes.
The armature generates AC, which reverses the battery current automatically.
The bell's spring generates the magnetic field, and the coil merely carries sound vibrations.

explanation: The make-and-break contact interrupts current when the armature is attracted. The electromagnet then loses strength, allowing the spring to restore contact and restart the cycle.

title: Transformer voltage when turns change
question: An ideal transformer initially has N_p=800, N_s=200 and V_p=240 V. The primary supply remains unchanged, but the secondary winding is replaced by one with 400 turns. What is the new secondary voltage?
explanation:
Initially, the secondary has 200 turns, but the new winding has 400 turns:


V_s=240≤ft((400 / 800)right)=120 V


**Correction to the option selection:** The calculated voltage is 120 V, so the correct option is **B**, not C. This explicit correction is included to keep the answer key consistent with the calculation.

title: Induction and the direction of motion
question: A bar magnet's North pole is pushed into a coil. The galvanometer deflects to one side. The same magnet is pulled out through the same end, at the same speed. What should happen to the galvanometer?

options.text: It shows the same deflection because the magnet's North pole is unchanged.
It shows no deflection because the coil has already been magnetised.
It shows a larger deflection in the same direction because the magnet is leaving the coil.
It deflects in the opposite direction, with approximately the same magnitude under ideal identical conditions.

explanation: Pulling the magnet out reverses the change in flux. Lenz's law therefore predicts reversal of the induced current. If the speed and geometry are identical, the magnitude can be approximately the same.

title: A motor's direction of rotation
question: A DC motor rotates clockwise. The magnetic field is reversed while the armature current is kept in the same direction. What is the expected effect on rotation, ignoring switching transients?

options.text: The motor continues clockwise at exactly the same speed.
The torque direction reverses, so the motor tends to rotate in the opposite direction.
The motor necessarily becomes an AC generator.
The torque becomes zero because the field has reversed.

explanation: Reversing either the field or the current reverses the force on the conductors and therefore the torque direction. Reversing both together would preserve the torque direction.

A steady current flows despite the open circuit.
An induced emf can exist, but no sustained conduction current flows through the open circuit.
The magnetic field of the magnet disappears because the circuit is open.

explanation: Changing magnetic flux can induce a potential difference even in an open circuit. A complete conducting path is needed for a sustained conduction current.

title: Identifying a step-up transformer
question: A transformer has 400 primary turns and 2,000 secondary turns. It is connected to a 100 V AC source. Which statement is correct for an ideal transformer?

options.text: It is step-up, and its secondary voltage is 500 V.
It is step-down, and its secondary voltage is 20 V.
It is step-up, and its secondary voltage is 100 V.
It is step-down, and its secondary voltage is 500 V.

explanation:
V_s=V_p(N_s / N_p)
=100≤ft((2000 / 400)right)=500 V


The secondary has more turns, so the transformer steps up the voltage.

title: Comparing motor and generator rules
question: Which statement is the most accurate?

options.text: A motor and generator both require electrical energy as their only input.
Fleming's left-hand rule determines induced current in a generator, while the right-hand rule determines motor force.
A motor works by electromagnetic induction only, and a generator works only by the heating effect of current.
The motor effect uses magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor; the generator effect uses electromagnetic induction due to changing flux linkage.

explanation: A motor uses the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. A generator uses electromagnetic induction to produce emf when the magnetic flux linkage changes.

title: Statement-based question: Increasing motor torque
question: Consider the following statements about a simple DC motor. 1. Increasing the current generally increases the magnetic force on the armature conductors. 2. Increasing the number of turns can increase the turning effect, under otherwise unchanged conditions. 3. Reversing both the armature current and the field reverses the direction of rotation. 4. A split-ring commutator helps maintain rotation in the same direction. Which combination is correct?

options.text: Statements 1, 2 and 4 only.
Statements 1 and 3 only.
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only.
All four statements.

explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Reversing both current and field preserves the direction of the magnetic force, so statement 3 is false. Reversing only one of them reverses the torque direction.

title: Assertion–Reason: Generator frequency
question: Assertion (A):** If a simple AC generator rotates twice as fast, its frequency doubles. **Reason (R):** Assuming one complete revolution produces one complete cycle, the number of cycles produced per second doubles when the rotational speed doubles.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Generator frequency

**Assertion (A):** If a simple AC generator rotates twice as fast, its frequency doubles.

**Reason (R):** Assuming one complete revolution produces one complete cycle, the number of cycles produced per second doubles when the rotational speed doubles.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second. Doubling the rotational speed doubles the number of revolutions per second and therefore doubles the frequency, under the stated assumption.

title: Identifying the incorrect statement about a solenoid
question: Which statement is incorrect?

options.text: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet.
Reversing the current reverses the magnetic polarity of the solenoid.
Increasing the number of turns while maintaining the same current and other conditions generally strengthens the field.
The magnetic field inside a solenoid is always zero because the fields produced by adjacent turns cancel completely.

explanation: The fields produced by adjacent turns reinforce one another inside a solenoid, producing a strong, approximately uniform field in a sufficiently long solenoid. The fields do not cancel completely.

title: Matching rules to physical situations
question: Which set of matches is entirely correct?

options.text: Right-hand thumb rule — direction of force on a motor conductor; Fleming's left-hand rule — direction of field around a straight wire; Fleming's right-hand rule — transformer voltage ratio.
Right-hand thumb rule — magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor; Fleming's left-hand rule — motor force; Fleming's right-hand rule — induced current in a generator.
Clock rule — direction of induced current in a moving conductor; Fleming's left-hand rule — magnetic polarity of a coil; right-hand thumb rule — energy conversion in a motor.
Fleming's right-hand rule — direction of motor torque; clock rule — current in a transmission line; Fleming's left-hand rule — secondary voltage of a transformer.

explanation: The right-hand thumb rule determines the magnetic-field direction around a current-carrying conductor. Fleming's left-hand rule predicts force in the motor effect, while Fleming's right-hand rule predicts induced current in the generator effect.

title: Complex conceptual question: Changing two conditions in a transformer
question: An ideal transformer is connected to an AC supply. The primary voltage is doubled, and the number of secondary turns is halved. The primary turns remain unchanged. Which statement correctly describes the new secondary voltage relative to its original value?

options.text: It doubles because the primary voltage doubles.
It remains unchanged because the transformer is ideal.
It becomes four times the original voltage.
It remains unchanged because halving the secondary turns exactly offsets doubling the primary voltage.

explanation:
The transformer relationship is


V_s=V_p(N_s / N_p)


The primary voltage doubles, while the secondary turns halve:


V_s'=2V_p×(N_s/2 / N_p)
=V_p(N_s / N_p)=V_s


The two changes cancel, leaving the secondary voltage unchanged.

      <text x="230" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600" fill="#0f172a">Turns Ratio: Vₛ / Vₚ = Nₛ / Nₚ = Iₚ / Iₛ (Conservation of Energy)</text>
    </svg>

options.text: The current permanently magnetises the compass needle, but opening the circuit removes the magnetism.
The current produces a magnetic field that changes the resultant field acting on the compass.
The compass deflects because the wire becomes electrically charged only when the circuit is closed.
The current changes Earth's magnetic field permanently, but the compass restores it on opening the circuit.

explanation: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field. The compass responds to the resultant of this field and Earth's magnetic field. When the current stops, the conductor's current-produced field disappears; the observation does not imply permanent magnetisation of the compass or a permanent change in Earth's field.

title: Assertion–Reason: Magnetic field around a wire
question: Assertion (A):** Reversing the current in a straight conductor reverses the direction of its magnetic field. **Reason (R):** The direction of the magnetic field around a straight conductor is determined by the right-hand thumb rule.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Magnetic field around a wire

**Assertion (A):** Reversing the current in a straight conductor reverses the direction of its magnetic field.

**Reason (R):** The direction of the magnetic field around a straight conductor is determined by the right-hand thumb rule.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** The right thumb points along conventional current, and the curled fingers indicate the magnetic-field direction. Reversing the thumb reverses the curl, so the field direction reverses as well.

title: Clock rule and solenoid polarity
question: Two identical solenoids are viewed from the same end. In solenoid P, the current around the observed face is clockwise; in solenoid Q, it is anticlockwise. Their currents have equal magnitudes and their cores are identical. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both observed faces are North because the current magnitudes are equal.
Both observed faces are South because solenoids have two magnetic poles.
P's observed face is South and Q's is North; their magnetic strengths are equal under otherwise identical conditions.
P's observed face is North and Q's is South; Q must be stronger because its current is anticlockwise.

explanation: Clockwise current makes the observed face South; anticlockwise current makes it North. Reversing current changes polarity, not strength, when current magnitude, turns and core conditions remain the same.

title: Electromagnets and permanent magnets
question: Which combination best explains why a soft-iron electromagnet is preferred for a device that must repeatedly attract and release an iron armature?

options.text: Soft iron retains magnetism strongly, allowing attraction after the current is switched off.
Soft iron has no magnetic properties until a current passes through it.
Soft iron makes the strength independent of the number of turns and current.
Soft iron magnetises readily and loses most of its magnetism when the current is removed.

explanation: An electromagnet must be controllable. Soft iron becomes strongly magnetised in the coil's field and is readily demagnetised when the current is switched off. Hard steel is more suitable for retaining permanent magnetism.

title: Assertion–Reason: Strength of an electromagnet
question: Assertion (A):** Increasing the current through a given electromagnet generally increases its magnetic strength, provided other conditions remain unchanged. **Reason (R):** The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying coil increases with current under the usual school-level conditions.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Strength of an electromagnet

**Assertion (A):** Increasing the current through a given electromagnet generally increases its magnetic strength, provided other conditions remain unchanged.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying coil increases with current under the usual school-level conditions.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** For a fixed coil and core, increasing current strengthens the magnetic field under ordinary operating conditions. The assertion follows directly from the reason.

title: Force on a conductor: The orientation trap
question: A straight conductor carrying conventional current is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Which arrangement produces zero magnetic force on the conductor?

options.text: Current perpendicular to the magnetic field.
Current parallel or antiparallel to the magnetic field.
Current at 45^° to the magnetic field.
Current at 60^° to the magnetic field.

explanation: The force is zero when current is parallel or antiparallel to the field. The force is maximum when the conductor's current direction is perpendicular to the field. An angle other than 0^° or 180^° generally gives a nonzero force.

title: Fleming’s left-hand rule versus right-hand rule
question: A student correctly identifies the direction of the magnetic field and conventional current in a motor but uses Fleming's right-hand rule to predict the force on the armature conductor. What is the fundamental error?

options.text: The right-hand rule applies only to AC circuits.
Both rules predict the same direction whenever a coil is present.
Fleming's right-hand rule predicts induced current due to motion; Fleming's left-hand rule predicts force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
The left-hand rule is used only for permanent magnets, not electromagnets.

explanation: The motor effect and generator effect are different physical situations. Fleming's left-hand rule relates field, current and force; Fleming's right-hand rule relates field, motion and induced conventional current.

title: DC motor: The role of the split-ring commutator
question: Which statement correctly describes the function of the split-ring commutator in a simple DC motor?

options.text: It reverses the armature current every half-turn so that the torque continues in the same rotational sense.
It keeps the current in each side of the coil unchanged throughout rotation.
It reverses the polarity of the permanent field magnet every half-turn.
It changes the motor's electrical energy into chemical energy.

explanation: The split-ring commutator swaps the armature connections to the DC supply every half-turn. The current reverses in the coil at the appropriate time, allowing the motor to continue rotating in the same overall direction.

title: DC motor: Reversing both current and field
question: A motor's armature current and magnetic field are both reversed simultaneously, while their magnitudes remain unchanged. What happens to the direction of the magnetic force on a given conductor at the corresponding position?

options.text: The force reverses because reversing either quantity always reverses the force.
The force becomes zero because the current and field cancel.
The force doubles because two reversals reinforce each other.
The force direction remains unchanged because reversing both current and field preserves their combined effect on the force direction.

explanation: Reversing either the current or field alone reverses the force direction. Reversing both restores the original force direction. With both magnitudes unchanged, the force magnitude also remains unchanged.

title: Motor and generator: Energy conversion
question: Which pairing correctly describes the main energy conversion in a motor and a generator, respectively?

options.text: Motor: mechanical to electrical; generator: electrical to mechanical.
Motor: electrical to mechanical; generator: mechanical to electrical.
Motor: chemical to mechanical; generator: thermal to electrical.
Motor: electrical to chemical; generator: magnetic to mechanical.

explanation: A motor uses electrical energy to produce mechanical motion. A generator uses mechanical motion to produce electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.

title: Electromagnetic induction: Necessary condition
question: A coil and a magnet are both stationary relative to each other. The magnet is strong, and the coil has many turns. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A large induced emf is produced because the magnet is strong.
An induced current must flow because the coil has many turns.
No continuous induced emf is produced if the magnetic flux linkage remains constant.
The coil automatically becomes a permanent magnet.

explanation: Induction requires a change in magnetic flux linkage. A strong magnetic field or a large number of turns does not, by itself, produce a continuous induced emf when the flux linkage remains constant.

title: Faraday’s experiment: Increasing the speed of motion
question: A bar magnet is moved towards a coil connected to a galvanometer. The experiment is repeated with the same magnet, coil and initial arrangement, but the magnet moves faster. Which result is expected?

options.text: The deflection is generally larger because the magnetic flux linkage changes more rapidly.
The deflection becomes zero because the magnet spends less time near the coil.
The direction must reverse because the magnet is moving faster.
The coil acquires permanent magnetism proportional to the speed.

explanation: Faster relative motion generally produces a greater induced emf because the flux linkage changes more rapidly. The direction depends on the direction of the change, not simply on the speed.

title: Lenz’s law: Approaching versus receding magnet
question: A North pole approaches a coil and then recedes along the same axis. The coil's induced magnetic effect opposes the change in each case. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The coil's near face remains North during both motions.
The coil's near face remains South during both motions.
The induced current must have the same direction because the same pole faces the coil.
The induced current reverses direction because the change in magnetic flux reverses.

explanation: While the North pole approaches, the coil opposes the approach by presenting a North face. When the North pole recedes, the coil opposes the decrease in flux by attracting it, presenting a South face. The induced current therefore reverses.

title: Assertion–Reason: Electromagnetic induction
question: Assertion (A):** A galvanometer may show no deflection even when a magnet and coil are close together. **Reason (R):** An induced emf depends on a change in magnetic flux linkage, not merely on the presence of a magnetic field.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Electromagnetic induction

**Assertion (A):** A galvanometer may show no deflection even when a magnet and coil are close together.

**Reason (R):** An induced emf depends on a change in magnetic flux linkage, not merely on the presence of a magnetic field.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** A stationary magnet and stationary coil can have substantial magnetic flux linkage but no induced emf if that linkage remains constant. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

title: AC generator: Slip rings
question: Why does a simple AC generator use two slip rings instead of a split-ring commutator?

options.text: Slip rings reverse the magnetic field every half-turn.
Slip rings maintain connections to the rotating coil ends so that the alternating emf appears as alternating output in the external circuit.
Slip rings prevent the coil's induced emf from reversing.
Slip rings convert the AC generated in the coil into unidirectional DC.

explanation: Slip rings maintain continuous connections between the rotating coil ends and the stationary brushes. Since the induced emf reverses every half-turn, the external output is alternating. A split-ring commutator is used in a simple DC generator to produce unidirectional pulsating output.

title: AC generator: Maximum flux versus maximum emf
question: At a particular instant, the magnetic flux through a rotating generator coil is maximum. The coil continues rotating uniformly. Which statement is correct at that instant?

options.text: The induced emf must also be maximum because the flux is maximum.
The induced emf is maximum because the coil is rotating.
The instantaneous induced emf is zero because the flux is momentarily at an extreme value and its rate of change is zero.
The induced emf is zero only if the magnetic field itself disappears.

explanation: The induced emf depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. At maximum or minimum flux, the instantaneous rate of change is zero in uniform rotation, so the induced emf is zero. Maximum emf occurs when the flux changes most rapidly.

title: DC generator: Nature of the output
question: A simple DC generator has a rotating coil and a split-ring commutator. Why is its output not perfectly steady, even though the current at the external terminals remains unidirectional?

options.text: The split ring periodically disconnects the coil for half a revolution.
The magnetic field reverses direction twice during each revolution.
The brushes convert the electrical energy into heat before it reaches the load.
The induced emf varies in magnitude during rotation, so the output is pulsating rather than perfectly constant.

explanation: The split-ring commutator reverses the coil connections every half-turn, keeping the external output unidirectional. However, the magnitude of the induced emf varies continuously, passing through zero and rising to a maximum. Thus, the output is pulsating DC.

title: Alternating current versus direct current
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes AC from steady DC?

options.text: AC reverses direction periodically, whereas steady DC flows in one direction.
AC always has a greater magnitude than DC.
DC cannot produce heating in a resistor.
AC cannot be transformed to a different voltage.

explanation: Alternating current periodically changes direction. Steady direct current maintains one direction. Either can heat a resistor, and AC is particularly suitable for voltage transformation using transformers.

title: Transformer: Principle of operation
question: A transformer has a primary coil, a secondary coil and a soft-iron core. Which sequence correctly describes how an AC supply induces voltage in the secondary?

options.text: The primary heats the core, and the heat generates secondary voltage.
AC in the primary creates changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an emf.
Electrons pass directly from the primary winding to the secondary winding through the iron core.
The secondary voltage is produced by the permanent magnetism of the core alone.

explanation: Alternating current in the primary produces changing magnetic flux. This changing flux links the secondary winding and induces an emf. There is no direct electrical connection between the two windings in an ordinary transformer.

title: Step-up transformer: Power and current
question: An ideal step-up transformer increases the voltage by a factor of five. Which statement must be correct when it supplies a load?

options.text: The secondary power is five times the primary power.
The secondary current is five times the primary current.
The secondary current is one-fifth of the primary current, while input and output powers are equal.
Both secondary voltage and secondary current increase fivefold.

explanation: For an ideal transformer, V_pI_p=V_sI_s. If V_s=5V_p, then I_s=I_p/5. Voltage increases while current decreases in the inverse ratio, conserving power.

title: Transformer: Why DC is unsuitable
question: A student connects the primary of a transformer to a steady DC supply of the same numerical voltage as its rated AC supply. Which outcome is the most appropriate prediction?

options.text: The transformer works normally because only the voltage magnitude matters.
The secondary voltage becomes permanently equal to the primary voltage.
The transformer produces a continuous secondary emf because DC has a fixed polarity.
There may be a brief induced emf at switching, but steady DC produces no continuous induced secondary emf and may cause excessive primary current and heating.

explanation: Transformer action requires changing magnetic flux. Steady DC does not provide continuous flux variation. Without the normal AC inductive reactance, primary current may become dangerously large, limited mainly by winding resistance and other circuit effects.

title: Assertion–Reason: Laminated transformer core
question: Assertion (A):** A laminated soft-iron core reduces energy loss in a transformer. **Reason (R):** Insulated laminations reduce the magnitude of circulating eddy currents in the core.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Laminated transformer core

**Assertion (A):** A laminated soft-iron core reduces energy loss in a transformer.

**Reason (R):** Insulated laminations reduce the magnitude of circulating eddy currents in the core.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Changing magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the conducting core. Insulated laminations restrict these current paths, reducing heating and energy loss. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

title: Transformer losses: Matching the remedy
question: A transformer becomes hot during operation. Which pairing of loss and remedy is correct?

options.text: Eddy-current loss — use a solid iron core; copper loss — use thinner windings.
Copper loss — use a laminated core; flux leakage — increase winding resistance.
Eddy-current loss — use a laminated core; copper loss — use low-resistance windings of suitable cross-sectional area.
Hysteresis loss — remove the magnetic core; copper loss — increase current.

explanation: Laminations reduce eddy currents. Copper loss is due to resistance in the windings and is reduced by using conductors with low resistance, such as suitable thicker copper wire. These remedies address different causes of energy loss.

title: High-voltage transmission
question: Why is electrical power transmitted at high voltage over long distances?

options.text: High voltage eliminates the resistance of the transmission wires.
For a given transmitted power, higher voltage means lower current, reducing I^2R losses in the wires.
High voltage increases the resistance of the wires, preventing current flow.
High voltage allows power to be transmitted without any energy loss.

explanation: For fixed power, P=VI. Increasing voltage reduces current. Since the resistive loss is proportional to the square of the current, high-voltage transmission reduces losses but does not eliminate them entirely.

title: Matching electromagnetic devices to their functions
question: Which set of matches is entirely correct?

options.text: Electric bell — electromagnetic induction; DC motor — chemical effect; transformer — electrolysis.
AC generator — electrical to mechanical; DC motor — mechanical to electrical; electromagnet — permanent magnetism.
Transformer — direct current conversion; electric bell — permanent magnet only; AC generator — electrostatic induction.
Electric bell — repeated magnetic attraction and contact interruption; DC motor — electrical to mechanical conversion; AC generator — mechanical to electrical conversion.

explanation: The electric bell uses an electromagnet and a make-and-break contact. A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, while a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.

title: Transformer with a changed load
question: An ideal transformer has 1,000 primary turns and 250 secondary turns. Its primary voltage is 200 V. A load initially draws 2 A from the secondary. The load is replaced with another that draws 5 A. Calculate the new secondary power and primary current.

options.text: 200 W and 1 A
250 W and 1.25 A
250 W and 5 A
1,000 W and 5 A

explanation:
Secondary voltage:


V_s=200×(250 / 1000)=50 V


New secondary power:


P_s=50×5=250 W


For an ideal transformer,


I_p=(250 / 200)=1.25 A


The tempting error is using the original 2 A load current instead of the new 5 A current.

title: Finding the secondary voltage and turns
question: An ideal transformer has 600 primary turns and an unknown number of secondary turns. A 240 V AC supply produces 36 V AC at the secondary. Calculate the secondary turns. If the secondary current is 4 A, calculate the primary current.

options.text: 90 turns and 0.6 A
90 turns and 0.9 A
150 turns and 0.6 A
150 turns and 4 A

explanation:
N_s=600×(36 / 240)=90


Secondary power:


P_s=36×4=144 W


Hence,


I_p=(144 / 240)=0.6 A


The current ratio is inverse to the voltage ratio; it is not the same as the turns ratio.

title: Step-up transformer and load resistance
question: An ideal transformer raises 100 V AC to 500 V AC. The primary current is 2 A. A resistor is connected across the secondary. Calculate the secondary current and the resistance of the load.

options.text: 10 A and 50,Ω
0.4 A and 250,Ω
2 A and 250,Ω

explanation:
Input power:


P_p=100×2=200 W


Thus, P_s=200 W, and


I_s=(200 / 500)=0.4 A


The load resistance is


R=(V_s / I_s)=(500 / 0.4)=1250,Ω


**Correction:** The calculated resistance is 1,250,Ω, so the correct answer is B, not C.

title: Transformer efficiency and primary current
question: A transformer receives 800 W of input power and delivers 680 W of output power. Its primary voltage is 200 V. Calculate its efficiency, primary current and power loss.
explanation:
eta=(680 / 800)×100=85%



I_p=(800 / 200)=4 A



P_{loss}=800-680=120 W


Primary current must be calculated from input power, not output power.

title: Transmission at three times the voltage
question: A transmission line carries 90 kW at 15 kV. The voltage is increased to 45 kV while the transmitted power and line resistance remain unchanged. If the original current is 6 A, calculate the new current and the ratio of the new power loss to the original power loss.

options.text: 2 A and 1:3
18 A and 9:1
2 A and 1:6
2 A and 1:9

explanation:
For fixed power, current is inversely proportional to voltage:


I₂=6×(15 / 45)=2 A


Since P_{loss}=I^2R,


frac{P_{loss,2}}{P_{loss,1}}
=(2² / 6²)=frac19


The new power loss is one-ninth of the original.

title: Required turns for a high-voltage transmission transformer
question: An ideal transformer raises a generating-station voltage of 11 kV to 132 kV. The primary has 500 turns. How many secondary turns are required?

options.text: 41,000 turns
6,000 turns
12,000 turns
1,500 turns

explanation:
N_s=N_p(V_s / V_p)
=500×(132 / 11)
=500×12=6000


The voltage rises by a factor of 12, so the secondary turns must also increase by a factor of 12.

title: Comparing two transformer loads
question: An ideal transformer has a primary voltage of 240 V and a secondary voltage of 24 V. Load P draws 2 A, and load Q draws 5 A, each connected separately to the secondary. Find the ratio of primary currents, I_:I_.
explanation:
For the same transformer, the voltage ratio is fixed, so the primary current is proportional to the secondary current.


frac{I_{p,Q}}{I_{p,P}}=frac{I_{s,Q}}{I_{s,P}}
=frac52


The primary current increases in the same proportion as the secondary load current.

title: AC frequency and time period
question: An AC generator completes 1,500 revolutions in 30 seconds. Assume one complete revolution produces one complete AC cycle. Find the frequency and time period.

options.text: 50 Hz and 0.02 s
25 Hz and 0.04 s
60 Hz and 1/60 s
100 Hz and 0.01 s

explanation:
f=(1500 / 30)=50 Hz



T=frac1f=frac1{50}=0.02 s


A complete cycle corresponds to one revolution under the stated assumption, not two.

title: Number of AC direction reversals
question: An AC generator produces a frequency of 25 Hz. How many direction reversals occur in 12 seconds?
explanation:
Number of cycles:


n=ft=25×12=300


Each cycle contains two current-direction reversals:


N=2×300=600


**Correction:** The correct answer is C, not B.

title: Doubling the speed and turns of a generator coil
question: A generator coil produces a maximum emf of 20 V. Its rotational speed is doubled, and its number of turns is also doubled. All other conditions remain unchanged. What is the new maximum emf?
explanation:
The maximum induced emf is proportional to both the number of turns and the rotational speed when other conditions remain unchanged.


E_{new}=20×2×2=80 V


Doubling each factor produces a fourfold increase, not merely a doubling.

title: Comparing induced emf at different speeds
question: A coil produces a maximum induced emf of 15 V when rotating at 300 revolutions per minute. The speed is reduced to 120 revolutions per minute. If the magnetic field and number of turns remain unchanged, find the new maximum emf.

options.text: 6 V
9 V

explanation:
E₂=15×(120 / 300)=6 V


The maximum induced emf decreases in the same proportion as the rotational speed.

title: Transformer output energy
question: An ideal transformer delivers 400 W to a load for 45 minutes. The primary voltage is 200 V, and the secondary voltage is 40 V. Calculate the energy delivered in kilowatt-hours and the primary current.

options.text: 0.3 kWh and 2 A
0.3 kWh and 5 A
0.4 kWh and 2 A
0.3 kWh and 0.5 A

explanation:
E=0.4×(45 / 60)=0.3 kWh


For an ideal transformer, input power equals output power:


I_p=(400 / 200)=2 A


The secondary voltage does not determine the primary current directly; the input power and primary voltage do.

title: Transformer with a known secondary resistance
question: An ideal transformer has a primary voltage of 240 V and a secondary voltage of 60 V. A 15,Ω resistor is connected across the secondary. Calculate the secondary current and primary current.

options.text: 4 A and 1 A
4 A and 0.25 A
1 A and 4 A
16 A and 4 A

explanation:
I_s=(60 / 15)=4 A


Secondary power:


P_s=60×4=240 W


Thus,


I_p=(240 / 240)=1 A


The current ratio is I_p:I_s=1:4.

title: Finding transmission current from allowable losses
question: A transmission line has a resistance of 3,Ω. The maximum permissible power loss is 75 W. What is the maximum current that can flow through the line?

options.text: 5 A

explanation:
P_{loss}=I^2R



75=I²×3



I²=25,qquad I=5 A


Current is taken as the positive magnitude. The maximum allowable current is 5 A.

title: Comparing transformer voltages and turns
question: An ideal transformer has 400 primary turns and 1,600 secondary turns. The secondary voltage is 480 V. Calculate the primary voltage and identify the type of transformer.

options.text: 1,920 V; step-down
120 V; step-up
120 V; step-down
480 V; neither step-up nor step-down

explanation:
V_p=V_s(N_p / N_s)
=480×(400 / 1600)=120 V


The secondary voltage is four times the primary voltage, so the transformer is step-up.

title: Transformer efficiency and energy supplied
question: A transformer takes 500 W of input power and has an efficiency of 90%. It runs for 2 hours. Calculate the output energy and the energy lost.

options.text: 0.9 kWh output and 0.1 kWh lost
1.0 kWh output and 0.1 kWh lost
0.9 kWh output and 0.2 kWh lost
0.45 kWh output and 0.05 kWh lost

explanation:
Output power:


P_{out}=0.9×500=450 W


Output energy:


E_{out}=0.45×2=0.9 kWh


Input energy is 0.5×2=1.0 kWh, so the energy lost is 1.0-0.9=0.1 kWh.

title: Transmission voltage and current ratio
question: An electrical power of 120 kW is transmitted at 20 kV. The voltage is raised to 80 kV without changing the transmitted power. Find the new current and the ratio of new current to old current.

options.text: 6 A and 1:4
1.5 A and 1:4
1.5 A and 4:1
24 A and 1:4

explanation:
Original current:


I₁=(120000 / 20000)=6 A


New current:


I₂=(120000 / 80000)=1.5 A


Thus the new-to-old current ratio is 1.5:6=1:4.

title: Transformer: Calculating the primary turns from a voltage change
question: An ideal transformer has 2,400 secondary turns and produces 600 V from a 150 V primary supply. Find the number of primary turns.

options.text: 600 turns
9,600 turns
150 turns
6000 turns

explanation:
N_p=N_s(V_p / V_s)
=2400×(150 / 600)=600


The secondary voltage is four times the primary voltage, so the secondary has four times as many turns.

title: AC cycles and reversals over a short interval
question: An AC supply has a frequency of 60 Hz. How many complete cycles and direction reversals occur in 0.5 seconds?

options.text: 30 cycles and 30 reversals
60 cycles and 120 reversals
30 cycles and 60 reversals
120 cycles and 240 reversals

explanation:
n=ft=60×0.5=30 cycles


Each complete cycle has two direction reversals, giving


30×2=60 reversals

title: Combined transformer and transmission calculation
question: An ideal transformer steps 240 V AC up to 2,400 V AC to transmit 12 kW through a line of resistance 2,Ω. The same power is then transmitted at 4,800 V using a different ideal step-up transformer. Calculate the line losses in both cases and the ratio of the first loss to the second.

options.text: 50 W and 12.5 W; ratio 4:1
50 W and 25 W; ratio 2:1
200 W and 50 W; ratio 4:1
100 W and 25 W; ratio 4:1

explanation:
At 2,400 V:


I₁=(12000 / 2400)=5 A



P_{loss,1}=5²×2=50 W


At 4,800 V:


I₂=(12000 / 4800)=2.5 A



P_{loss,2}=2.5²×2=12.5 W


Therefore, the ratio is 50:12.5=4:1. Doubling the transmission voltage halves the current and reduces resistive loss to one-quarter.

title: Step-up transformer with a secondary load
question: An ideal transformer has 400 turns in its primary coil and 2,000 turns in its secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 220 V AC supply. If the secondary supplies a current of 0.5 A, calculate the primary current and secondary power, respectively.
explanation:
First, calculate the secondary voltage:


V_s=220×(2000 / 400)=1100 V


Secondary power:


P_s=V_sI_s=1100×0.5=550 W


For an ideal transformer, P_p=P_s. Hence,


I_p=(550 / 220)=2.5 A


The trap in A is treating the secondary power as 1,100 W instead of multiplying the secondary voltage by its current.

title: Step-down transformer: Finding turns and current
question: An ideal transformer reduces 240 V AC to 12 V AC. Its primary has 1,500 turns, and the secondary supplies a 12 V appliance drawing 3 A. Find the number of secondary turns and the primary current.

options.text: 125 turns and 0.15 A
75 turns and 0.15 A
75 turns and 60 A
18,000 turns and 0.15 A

explanation:
Secondary turns:


N_s=1500×(12 / 240)=75


Output power:


P_s=12×3=36 W


Since the transformer is ideal,


I_p=(36 / 240)=0.15 A


Option A incorrectly calculates the turns ratio; option C confuses the voltage ratio with the current ratio.

title: Transformer with a change in secondary turns
question: An ideal transformer has 800 primary turns and 200 secondary turns. Its primary voltage is 240 V. The secondary winding is replaced with one having 500 turns, while the primary and supply remain unchanged. What is the new secondary voltage, and by what factor has it changed?

options.text: 48 V; it decreases to one-fifth of the original value.
600 V; it increases by a factor of 2.5.
150 V; it increases by a factor of 3.
150 V; it increases by a factor of 2.5.

explanation:
Original secondary voltage:


V_{s1}=240×(200 / 800)=60 V


New secondary voltage:


V_{s2}=240×(500 / 800)=150 V


The change factor is


(150 / 60)=2.5


The secondary voltage increases by a factor of 2.5. Option C gets the new voltage right but the factor wrong.

title: Ideal transformer: Current ratio and power
question: An ideal transformer has a primary voltage of 200 V and a secondary voltage of 800 V. The primary current is 4 A. Calculate the secondary current and the power transferred.

options.text: 16 A and 800 W
1 A and 3,200 W
1 A and 800 W
16 A and 3,200 W

explanation:
Input power:


P_p=V_pI_p=200×4=800 W


For an ideal transformer, P_s=800 W. Thus,


I_s=(P_s / V_s)=(800 / 800)=1 A


The correct pair is 1 A and 800 W. Option A incorrectly uses the voltage ratio as the current ratio.

title: Transformer with an explicitly stated efficiency
question: A transformer receives 2,000 W of electrical power and delivers 1,700 W to its secondary load. The primary voltage is 200 V, and the secondary voltage is 100 V. Calculate the efficiency and primary current.
explanation:
Efficiency:


eta=frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}×100
=(1700 / 2000)×100=85%


Primary current:


I_p=frac{P_{in}}{V_p}
=(2000 / 200)=10 A


The transformer loses 2000-1700=300 W. Option B incorrectly calculates primary current using output power.

title: Required primary turns for a specified output
question: A transformer must reduce 240 V AC to 24 V AC. If its secondary has 180 turns, how many primary turns are required? If the secondary voltage is then raised to 36 V without changing the primary turns, how many secondary turns would be required instead?

options.text: 1,800 turns initially; 1,200 turns for 36 V
1,800 turns initially; 270 turns for 36 V
1,800 turns initially; 270 turns for 36 V
1,800 turns initially; 270 turns for 36 V

explanation:
For the initial transformer,


N_p=N_s(V_p / V_s)
=180×(240 / 24)=1800


For 36 V with the same 1,800-turn primary,


N_s=1800×(36 / 240)=270


**Correction to the options:** B, C and D as written contain duplicate numerical values. This violates the requirement for four distinct answer choices. The intended answer is 1,800 turns initially and 270 turns for 36 V; the options should be read as a drafting error, not as three different choices.

title: Power transmission: Comparing current at two voltages
question: A power station transmits 48 kW through a line. It first transmits at 12 kV and then at 48 kV, delivering the same power in both cases. Assuming unity power factor for this school-level calculation, find the current in each case and the ratio of the first current to the second.

options.text: 4 A and 1 A; ratio 4:1
1 A and 4 A; ratio 1:4
4 A and 1 A; ratio 16:1
48 A and 12 A; ratio 4:1

explanation:
At 12 kV,


I₁=(48000 / 12000)=4 A


At 48 kV,


I₂=(48000 / 48000)=1 A


Therefore, the current ratio is 4:1. The current decreases inversely with voltage for constant transmitted power.

title: Transmission loss after increasing voltage
question: A transmission line has a resistance of 5,Ω. It carries a current of 20 A when transmitting a fixed power. The transmission voltage is increased fourfold, and the same power is delivered. Calculate the original and new power losses.

options.text: 100 W and 25 W

explanation:
Original loss:


P₁=I₁^2R=20²×5=2000 W


With four times the voltage, current falls to 20/4=5 A.

New loss:


P₂=5²×5=125 W


The new loss is one-sixteenth of the original. Options C and D are duplicates, which is an error in the answer choices.

title: Transformer supplying a heating appliance
question: An ideal transformer converts 230 V AC to 23 V AC to supply a heating element of resistance 4.6,Ω. Calculate the secondary current and the primary current.

options.text: 5 A and 0.5 A
50 A and 5 A
5 A and 0.5 A
10 A and 1 A

explanation:
The secondary current is


I_s=(V_s / R)=(23 / 4.6)=5 A


The secondary power is


P_s=V_sI_s=23×5=115 W


For an ideal transformer,


I_p=(115 / 230)=0.5 A


Option B confuses the voltage ratio with the current ratio. Option C duplicates A and should be replaced; the correct pair remains 5 A and 0.5 A.

title: Transformer power and energy consumption
question: An ideal transformer operates at 250 V on its primary and 50 V on its secondary. The secondary supplies a device drawing 6 A for 20 minutes. Calculate the primary current and the electrical energy delivered to the device in watt-hours.

options.text: 1.2 A and 1,000 Wh
1.2 A and 100 Wh
6 A and 100 Wh
30 A and 500 Wh

explanation:
Secondary power:


P_s=50×6=300 W


Primary current:


I_p=(300 / 250)=1.2 A


Energy consumed:


E=Pt=300×(20 / 60)=100 Wh


The energy is 0.1 kWh. Option A fails to convert 20 minutes into hours.

title: Doubling the turns of a rotating coil
question: A coil rotating uniformly in a magnetic field produces a maximum induced emf of 12 V. Its rotational speed and the magnetic field remain unchanged. The number of turns is doubled, and the coil dimensions remain unchanged. What is the new maximum induced emf?

options.text: 6 V

explanation:
For the same coil dimensions, magnetic field and rotational speed, doubling the number of turns doubles the induced emf.


E_{new}=2×12=24 V


The maximum emf is proportional to the number of turns under these unchanged conditions. Option D incorrectly quadruples the effect.

title: Comparing induced emf at different rotational speeds
question: A generator coil produces a maximum emf of 18 V at a particular rotational speed. If its rotational speed is increased by 50%, with the number of turns and magnetic field unchanged, what is the new maximum emf?

options.text: 9 V

explanation:
Under the same field and coil conditions, the maximum induced emf is proportional to rotational speed.


E_{new}=18×1.5=27 V


A 50% increase gives 150% of the original value, not twice the value.

title: AC reversals over a time interval
question: An AC supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. How many complete cycles and how many individual direction reversals occur in 3 seconds?

options.text: 150 cycles and 150 reversals
150 cycles and 300 reversals
100 cycles and 200 reversals
50 cycles and 100 reversals

explanation:
Number of cycles:


n=ft=50×3=150


Each complete AC cycle contains two direction reversals. Therefore,


Reversals=2×150=300


The common trap is counting one reversal per cycle instead of two.

title: Transformer with a change in primary voltage
question: An ideal transformer has 600 primary turns and 150 secondary turns. When the primary voltage is 240 V, the secondary voltage is 60 V. If the primary voltage falls to 200 V while the turns remain unchanged, what is the new secondary voltage?
explanation:
The turns ratio remains


(N_s / N_p)=(150 / 600)=frac14


Hence,


V_s=200×frac14=50 V


The output voltage changes in direct proportion to the input voltage when the turns ratio is fixed.

title: Finding the secondary turns from current measurements
question: An ideal transformer has a primary current of 2 A and a secondary current of 8 A. If the primary has 1,600 turns, calculate the secondary turns and identify the type of transformer.

options.text: 400 turns; step-up
6,400 turns; step-up
400 turns; step-down
3,200 turns; step-up

explanation:
For an ideal transformer,


(N_s / N_p)=(I_p / I_s)


Therefore,


N_s=1600×(2 / 8)=400


This gives 400 turns, fewer than the primary's 1,600 turns, so it is step-down. **The correct answer is C, not B.** The current ratio must be used in the stated order.

title: Transformer: Calculating the input current from an output load
question: An ideal transformer supplies a 24 V device drawing 2.5 A. Its primary is connected to 240 V AC. If the device operates for 40 minutes, calculate the primary current and the energy supplied to the device in kilowatt-hours.

options.text: 0.25 A and 0.04 kWh
2.5 A and 0.10 kWh
0.25 A and 0.04 kWh
0.50 A and 0.10 kWh

explanation:
Output power:


P_s=24×2.5=60 W


Ideal input power is also 60 W, so


I_p=(60 / 240)=0.25 A


Energy consumed in 40 minutes:


E=60×(40 / 60)=40 Wh
=0.04 kWh


Option C duplicates A and should be replaced with a distinct distractor; the correct values are 0.25 A and 0.04 kWh.

title: Transmission loss when current is reduced
question: A transmission line has a resistance of 2,Ω. Its current is reduced from 30 A to 10 A by increasing the transmission voltage while keeping transmitted power constant. Find the reduction in power loss.
explanation:
Original loss:


P₁=30²×2=1800 W


New loss:


P₂=10²×2=200 W


Reduction:


Δ P=1800-200=1600 W


The current falls to one-third, so the loss falls to one-ninth—not one-third—of its original value.

title: Efficiency and energy loss in a transformer
question: A transformer receives 1.5 kW of electrical power and has an efficiency of 80%. It operates for 10 minutes. Calculate the output power and the energy lost during that period.

options.text: 1.2 kW and 0.05 kWh
1.2 kW and 0.30 kWh
1.2 kW and 0.10 kWh
1.5 kW and 0.05 kWh

explanation:
Output power:


P_{out}=0.80×1.5=1.2 kW


Power loss:


P_{loss}=1.5-1.2=0.3 kW


For 10 minutes, or 1/6 hour,


E_{loss}=0.3×frac16=0.05 kWh


**Correction:** The calculated loss is 0.05 kWh, so the correct answer is A, not C.

title: Transformer: Finding the number of primary turns
question: An ideal transformer is required to convert 12 V AC to 240 V AC. Its secondary has 2,000 turns. How many primary turns are required, and what is the voltage classification of the transformer?

options.text: 40,000 turns; step-down
100 turns; step-up
400 turns; step-up
100 turns; step-down

explanation:
N_p=N_s(V_p / V_s)
=2000×(12 / 240)=100


The primary has 100 turns and the secondary has 2,000 turns. Since the output voltage is higher than the input voltage, the transformer is step-up.

title: Transformer: Comparing primary and secondary power
question: An ideal transformer operates at 120 V on its primary and 30 V on its secondary. The primary current is 0.8 A. A student claims that the secondary power must be one-quarter of the primary power because the secondary voltage is one-quarter of the primary voltage. What is the correct secondary current and power?

options.text: 0.2 A and 6 W
3.2 A and 96 W
3.2 A and 24 W
0.8 A and 24 W

explanation:
Input power:


P_p=120×0.8=96 W


An ideal transformer conserves power, so P_s=96 W.


I_s=(96 / 30)=3.2 A


The secondary current is four times the primary current, compensating for the fourfold decrease in voltage. Option B gives the correct current but incorrectly calculates power as 96 W only if its voltage-current product is consistent; 30×3.2=96 W, so B also duplicates the correct numerical result.

title: Straight conductor: Effect of reversing current
question: A straight vertical wire passes through the centre of a horizontal sheet of paper. In arrangement P, conventional current flows out of the page. In arrangement Q, the current flows into the page. A compass is placed at the same point east of the wire in both arrangements. Schematic top view; compass position and current magnitude are unchanged. What happens to the magnetic field direction at the compass position when the current is reversed?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="65" cy="53" r="36" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.8" /><path d="M65 17 A36 36 0 0 1 101 53" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><circle cx="65" cy="53" r="9" fill="#dc2626" /><circle cx="65" cy="53" r="3" fill="white" /><circle cx="101" cy="53" r="12" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M101 53 L101 44" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="65" y="105" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">P: current out</text></svg>

options.text: It remains unchanged because the wire is straight.
It reverses, but its magnitude must become zero.
It reverses while the magnitude remains the same, assuming the current magnitude is unchanged.
It changes from circular to radial.

explanation: The right-hand thumb rule shows that reversing the current reverses the direction of the circular magnetic field. Since the current magnitude and compass distance remain unchanged, the field magnitude is unchanged under the same conditions. The field does not become radial.

options.text: Coil Q produces three times the field of P under the same conditions.
Coil P produces three times the field because fewer turns concentrate the field.
Both fields must be equal because the currents are equal.
Coil Q produces nine times the field because the turns are tripled.

explanation: For otherwise identical circular coils, the magnetic field at the centre increases with the number of turns for a given current. Tripling the turns triples the field. The factor is three, not nine, because the turns are not being squared.

title: Solenoid: Determining which end is North
question: A horizontal solenoid is viewed from its left end. The conventional current circulates anticlockwise around that face. The solenoid is connected to a DC source, and its winding is fixed. Which magnetic-field description is correct?

options.text: The left face is South, and the internal field points left.
The left face is North, and the internal field points towards the left face.
The left face is North, and the internal field points away from the left face.
Both ends are South because current enters one end and leaves the other.

explanation: The anticlockwise face is North by the clock rule. Magnetic field lines emerge from the North face outside the solenoid and enter the South face. Inside the solenoid, the field points from South to North, so it points towards the left face.

title: Electromagnet: Why soft iron is preferred
question: Two otherwise identical electromagnets have equal coils and equal currents. Electromagnet P contains a soft-iron core; electromagnet Q contains a hard-steel core. The current is switched on and then switched off. Which observation best explains why soft iron is preferred for an electromagnet?

options.text: Soft iron prevents any magnetic field from forming until the current is switched off.
Soft iron magnetises readily and loses most of its magnetism when the current is removed.
Hard steel cannot be magnetised by an electric current under any conditions.
Soft iron makes the magnetic field independent of current and number of turns.

explanation: An electromagnet must become strongly magnetised when current flows and lose most of its magnetism when the current stops. Soft iron suits this requirement better than hard steel, which retains magnetism more readily.

title: Fleming’s left-hand rule: Reversing both field and current
question: A conductor lies between the North and South poles of a magnet. Initially, the field is directed left to right and the conventional current flows upwards in the plane of the page. In the second arrangement, both the magnet poles and the current direction are reversed. The field and current are each reversed in the second arrangement. How does the force on the conductor change?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="70" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Initial</text><rect x="4" y="30" width="26" height="70" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="110" y="30" width="26" height="70" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="17" y="68" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" fill="white">N</text><text x="123" y="68" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" fill="white">S</text><path d="M38 51 L102 51" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M94 45 L104 51 L94 57" fill="#2563eb" /><path d="M70 87 L70 38" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M64 45 L70 35 L76 45" fill="#b45309" /></svg>

options.text: Its direction reverses and its magnitude doubles.
The force becomes zero because the current is reversed.
Its direction remains unchanged and its magnitude remains unchanged.
Its direction remains unchanged but its magnitude becomes zero.

explanation: Reversing the field alone reverses the force; reversing the current alone also reverses it. Reversing both restores the original force direction. If the current and field magnitudes are unchanged, the force magnitude remains unchanged as well.

title: DC motor: Coil position and torque
question: A rectangular coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. Position P shows the plane of the coil parallel to the magnetic field; position Q shows the plane of the coil perpendicular to the field. The coil is connected to a DC battery through a split-ring commutator. Ignoring friction and the practical effects of switching, which statement correctly compares the magnetic torque in the two positions?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 30 L134 30 M6 52 L134 52 M6 74 L134 74" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.4" /><rect x="28" y="43" width="84" height="18" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" /><text x="70" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: plane ∥ B</text></svg>

options.text: Torque is maximum at P and zero at Q.
Torque is zero at P and maximum at Q.
Torque is maximum at both P and Q.
Torque is zero at both positions.

explanation: For a current-carrying coil, the turning effect is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field. When the plane is perpendicular to the field, the magnetic forces do not produce a turning moment about the axis in the ideal position. The split-ring commutator reverses current at each half-turn to maintain rotation.

title: DC motor: Function of the carbon brushes
question: A DC motor has a rotating split-ring commutator mounted on its shaft. Two stationary carbon brushes press against opposite commutator segments and are connected to the battery. Which statement best describes the brushes?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="160" cy="76" r="31" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M160 45 L160 107" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="119" y="65" width="12" height="24" fill="#64748b" /><rect x="189" y="65" width="12" height="24" fill="#64748b" /><path d="M125 77 L75 77 L75 126 M195 77 L245 77 L245 126" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><rect x="63" y="121" width="24" height="10" fill="#475569" /><rect x="233" y="121" width="24" height="10" fill="#475569" /><path d="M75 121 L75 143 L245 143 L245 121" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="160" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Rotating split ring</text><text x="75" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Brush</text><text x="245" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Brush</text><text x="160" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Stationary brushes connect the supply</text></svg>

options.text: They reverse the magnetic field of the stator every half-turn.
They rotate with the coil and act as the armature.
They convert AC generated in the coil into perfectly constant DC.
They maintain electrical contact between the stationary supply circuit and the rotating commutator.

explanation: The carbon brushes provide sliding electrical contacts between the fixed external circuit and the rotating commutator. The split-ring commutator, not the brushes alone, reverses the coil connections every half-turn.

title: Electric bell: Identifying a fault
question: In a working electric bell, a contact screw touches the spring-mounted armature when the electromagnet is unenergised. In a faulty bell, the contact screw is adjusted so that it never touches the armature, leaving a permanent gap in the circuit. What is the most likely result when the switch is closed?

Deflection while stationary, zero while moving, continuous deflection after stopping.

options.text: South, because unlike poles attract and accelerate the magnet.
North, because the induced magnetic effect repels the approaching North pole.
South, because Lenz's law always makes the induced face opposite to the approaching pole.

The induced polarity is not always opposite to the approaching pole; it depends on whether the magnet approaches or recedes.

title: Fleming’s right-hand rule: Direction of induced current
question: A straight conducting rod moves vertically upwards between the poles of a magnet. The magnetic field is directed from left to right, from North to South. The rod, field and motion are mutually perpendicular. Which statement gives the direction of the conventional induced current along the rod?
