options.text: Downwards, because the right-hand rule is used for motors.
Upwards, because the current follows the direction of motion.
No induced current is possible because the field is uniform.
Out of the page, because the right thumb points upwards, the first finger points right, and the second finger gives the current.

explanation: Fleming's right-hand rule uses the thumb for motion, the first finger for magnetic field and the second finger for conventional induced current. With motion upward and field to the right, the induced current is out of the page. This is the generator rule, not the motor rule.

question: A coil rotates uniformly in a magnetic field. At position P, the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. After rotating through 90^°, it reaches position Q, where the plane of the coil is parallel to the field. How does the magnitude of the induced emf change from P to Q?

It changes from zero to maximum.
It remains zero because the magnetic field is uniform.
It remains maximum because the coil is rotating uniformly.

explanation: At P, the coil's flux is momentarily maximum and its rate of change is zero, so the emf is zero. After a quarter-turn, at Q, the flux is momentarily zero but changes most rapidly, so the emf is maximum.

title: DC generator: Why the output is unidirectional
question: A rotating coil generates an alternating emf internally. Its ends connect to two halves of a split-ring commutator, with fixed brushes connected to an external circuit. The diagram shows the coil just after completing half a revolution. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="25" y="35" width="35" height="95" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="260" y="35" width="35" height="95" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="42" y="87" font-size="20" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">N</text><text x="277" y="87" font-size="20" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">S</text><rect x="91" y="49" width="138" height="66" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M160 115 L160 135" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M142 142 A18 18 0 0 1 160 124 L160 160 A18 18 0 0 1 142 142" fill="#b45309" /><path d="M160 124 A18 18 0 0 1 178 142 A18 18 0 0 1 160 160 Z" fill="#d97706" /><rect x="122" y="136" width="11" height="18" fill="#64748b" /><rect x="187" y="136" width="11" height="18" fill="#64748b" /><text x="160" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Rotating coil and split ring</text></svg>

options.text: The split ring reverses the external connections every half-turn, compensating for the reversal of emf within the coil.
The split ring prevents the emf in the coil from reversing.
The brushes reverse the magnet's polarity every half-turn.
The split ring works by stopping the coil at every zero-emf position.

explanation: The induced emf inside the coil reverses every half-turn. The split-ring commutator also swaps the coil ends connected to the brushes, maintaining the same polarity at the external terminals during successive half-cycles. The output is pulsating DC, not perfectly constant DC.

title: Transformer core: Identifying the purpose of lamination
question: Two transformer cores are compared. Core P is made of a solid block of iron; core Q is made of thin insulated iron sheets stacked together. Both transformers operate on the same AC supply. Why does core Q reduce energy loss?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 115" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="28" width="80" height="58" fill="#64748b" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2" /><text x="70" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">P: Solid core</text><text x="70" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Larger eddy-current loss</text></svg>

options.text: Insulation between sheets eliminates the need for a changing magnetic field.
Laminations increase the resistance of paths for circulating eddy currents, reducing their magnitude and associated heating.
Laminations convert AC into DC before it reaches the secondary.
Laminations prevent magnetic flux from entering the core.

explanation: A changing magnetic field induces circulating currents in a conducting core. Thin insulated laminations interrupt these paths and increase their effective resistance, reducing eddy-current heating. The transformer still requires changing magnetic flux.

title: Power transmission: Identifying the correct transformer sequence
question: Electricity leaves a generating station at 11 kV, travels through long transmission lines, and is finally supplied to homes at approximately 230 V. Ideal transformers are used at the relevant stages. Which statement best explains this sequence?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 330 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="43" width="67" height="49" rx="4" fill="#64748b" /><text x="41" y="63" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Generator</text><text x="41" y="78" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">11 kV</text><path d="M75 67 L102 67" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M95 61 L105 67 L95 73" fill="currentColor" /><rect x="106" y="43" width="56" height="49" rx="4" fill="#b45309" /><text x="134" y="63" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Step-up</text><text x="134" y="78" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">132 kV</text><path d="M162 67 L188 67" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M181 61 L191 67 L181 73" fill="currentColor" /><rect x="192" y="43" width="57" height="49" rx="4" fill="#64748b" /><text x="220" y="63" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Lines</text><text x="220" y="78" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">132 kV</text><path d="M249 67 L266 67" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M259 61 L269 67 L259 73" fill="currentColor" /><rect x="270" y="43" width="52" height="49" rx="4" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="296" y="63" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Step-down</text><text x="296" y="78" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">230 V</text><text x="165" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Transmission voltage is raised, then reduced for use</text></svg>

options.text: High voltage is used to increase the current in the transmission lines.
High voltage eliminates all electrical resistance in the wires.
High voltage is used because a step-up transformer creates additional energy.
High voltage reduces the current required to transmit a given power, thereby reducing resistive power loss; a step-down transformer then supplies a safer, useful voltage.

explanation: For fixed transmitted power, P=VI. Raising the voltage lowers the current. Since resistive losses are proportional to I^2R, this substantially reduces transmission losses. The receiving end steps the voltage down for distribution and domestic use.

title: Electromagnetic induction: Interpreting coil orientation and motion
question: A rectangular coil is connected to a galvanometer and placed between magnetic poles. In position P, the coil is rotated in the field. In position Q, the coil is held stationary with the same orientation. In position R, the coil is rotated at the same speed as in P, but its axis of rotation is aligned differently so that its magnetic flux linkage remains constant. All coils have the same number of turns and are in the same magnetic field. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M5 25 L95 25 M5 45 L95 45 M5 65 L95 65" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.2" /><rect x="30" y="24" width="40" height="43" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M50 72 L50 87" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M45 82 L50 90 L55 82" fill="currentColor" /><text x="50" y="13" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P: Rotating</text></svg>

options.text: All three produce the same induced emf because they are in a magnetic field.
P and R necessarily produce equal induced emfs because their rotation speeds are equal.
Q produces the greatest induced emf because its orientation does not change.
P produces an induced emf if its flux linkage changes; Q produces no continuous induced emf, and R produces none under the stated constant-flux-linkage condition.

explanation: Electromagnetic induction requires a change in magnetic flux linkage. Rotation can induce an emf when it changes the flux linkage, but rotation alone does not guarantee induction. A stationary coil with constant flux linkage has no continuous induced emf. Likewise, the specified rotation in R produces no induced emf if the flux linkage remains constant.

explanation:
correctly describes the expected behaviour?

C) DC cannot flow through a coil because the coil has inductance.

D) DC produces normal transformer action, but the secondary current flows in the same direction forever.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:** Transformer action requires a changing magnetic flux linking the secondary. When a DC supply is first switched on or off, the flux changes briefly and a transient emf may be induced. With steady DC, the flux becomes constant and the induced secondary emf falls to zero. AC continuously changes the flux.

title: Power transmission: Comparing energy losses
question: The same electrical power is transmitted through identical transmission wires in two separate cases. Case P uses a low transmission voltage and Case Q uses a much higher transmission voltage. Both systems deliver the same useful power to their loads. If the transmission voltage in Case Q is four times that in Case P, what is the ratio of power lost in the wires, P_:P_?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 175" width="100%">

    <rect x="187" y="40" width="48" height="32" fill="#64748b" rx="3"/><rect x="263" y="40" width="48" height="32" fill="#64748b" rx="3"/>
    <path d="M235 48 L263 48 M235 64 L263 64" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>

    <text x="211" y="60" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Supply</text><text x="287" y="60" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">Load</text>
    <text x="80" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Lower V, higher I</text>
    <text x="248" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Higher V, lower I</text>
    <path d="M24 118 L136 118 M194 118 L306 118" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="4"/>

    <text x="248" y="143" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Same wire resistance</text>
    <text x="165" y="165" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Equal transmitted power</text>

explanation:
For equal transmitted power, P=VI, so quadrupling the voltage reduces the current to one-quarter.

For identical wires, power loss is proportional to I^2R. Hence,


frac{P_{loss,P}}{P_{loss,Q}}
=(I_P² / I_Q²)
=(I_P² / (I_P/4)²)=16


The loss in Case P is 16 times the loss in Case Q.

title: Oersted’s experiment: Predicting compass deflection
question: A straight wire passes vertically above a compass. The conventional current flows vertically upward, out of the page when viewed from below. The compass needle is initially aligned along the north–south direction. Red and blue indicate the initial north and south ends of the compass needle. If the wire is placed directly above the compass and the current is switched on, which conclusion is scientifically justified?

The needle's north pole always points in the direction of conventional current.

explanation: Oersted demonstrated that an electric current produces a magnetic field. The compass responds to the resultant magnetic field, which depends on both the wire's field and Earth's field. A 90^° deflection is not guaranteed, and the compass needle does not simply point along the current.

title: Fleming’s left-hand rule: Direction of force
question: The magnetic field between two pole pieces is directed from left to right. A straight conductor carries conventional current vertically upward in the plane of the page. What is the direction of the force on the conductor?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="arr6" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 Z" fill="#2563eb" /></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="32" width="45" height="115" rx="4" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="255" y="32" width="45" height="115" rx="4" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="42" y="91" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="white">N</text><text x="278" y="91" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="white">S</text><path d="M76 78 L243 78" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arr6)" /><text x="160" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">B: left to right</text><path d="M160 133 L160 40" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M152 51 L160 37 L168 51 Z" fill="#b45309" /><text x="173" y="127" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">I upward</text><text x="160" y="169" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Conductor in the plane of the page</text></svg>

options.text: Vertically upward.
Into the page.
To the left.
Out of the page.

explanation: In Fleming’s left-hand rule, the first finger points right (field), the second finger points up (conventional current), and the thumb gives the force. The force is into the page. The right-hand rule is used for generators, not motors.

question: A conductor can slide between the pole pieces of a magnet. Position P shows the conductor parallel to the magnetic field; position Q shows it perpendicular to the field. The same current flows in both positions. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: The force is zero in P and greatest in Q.
The force is greatest in P and zero in Q.
The force is equal in both positions because the current is unchanged.
The force is zero in both positions because the conductor is straight.

explanation: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor depends on its orientation relative to the field. It is zero when current is parallel to the field and maximum when current is perpendicular to it. Thus, P experiences no magnetic force while Q experiences the maximum force for the given current and field.

title: DC motor: Identifying the split-ring commutator
question: A simple DC motor has a rectangular armature coil ABCD between North and South poles. Its two coil ends connect to separate halves of a split-ring commutator, which touch stationary carbon brushes connected to a DC battery. What is the essential function of the split-ring commutator?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 220" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="46" width="48" height="112" rx="4" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="278" y="46" width="48" height="112" rx="4" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="38" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="white">N</text><text x="302" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="white">S</text><rect x="98" y="70" width="145" height="68" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><text x="94" y="65" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="245" y="65" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">B</text><text x="94" y="153" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">D</text><text x="245" y="153" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">C</text><path d="M170 138 L170 166" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M156 170 A14 14 0 0 1 170 156 L170 184 A14 14 0 0 1 156 170 Z" fill="#b45309" /><path d="M170 156 A14 14 0 0 1 184 170 A14 14 0 0 1 170 184 Z" fill="#d97706" /><rect x="139" y="164" width="10" height="28" fill="#64748b" /><rect x="191" y="164" width="10" height="28" fill="#64748b" /><path d="M144 192 L144 204 L104 204" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M196 192 L196 204 L236 204" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="170" y="17" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Armature coil</text><text x="170" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Split-ring commutator and brushes</text></svg>

options.text: It reverses the magnetic field of the permanent magnets every half-turn.
It keeps the current in the armature coil unchanged in direction throughout rotation.
It converts the battery’s DC into AC before the current enters the coil.
It reverses the current in the armature coil every half-turn so that the torque continues in the same rotational sense.

explanation: The split-ring commutator swaps the coil's connections to the battery every half-turn. This reverses the coil current when the sides exchange positions, maintaining rotation in the same overall direction. Slip rings, by contrast, are used in an AC generator to maintain continuous connections to the rotating coil.

title: DC motor: What happens if the battery terminals are reversed?
question: A DC motor is rotating clockwise when viewed from its front. The North and South poles of its field magnet remain fixed. The battery connections are then reversed without changing the magnet or the motor's construction. Assuming the motor is connected correctly and starts rotating, what happens to its direction of rotation?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="arr9" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 Z" fill="#b45309" /></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="42" width="48" height="95" rx="4" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="252" y="42" width="48" height="95" rx="4" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="44" y="94" font-size="22" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">N</text><text x="276" y="94" font-size="22" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">S</text><rect x="104" y="57" width="112" height="67" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M160 90 A32 32 0 1 1 159 89" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arr9)" /><text x="160" y="19" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Battery polarity reversed</text><text x="160" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Field magnet unchanged</text></svg>

options.text: It remains clockwise because the field magnet is unchanged.
It reverses because the current in the armature reverses while the field direction stays fixed.
It stops permanently because the split-ring commutator cannot operate with reversed polarity.
It reverses only if the field magnet is also reversed.

explanation: Reversing the battery reverses the armature current. With the magnetic field unchanged, the force on each side of the coil reverses, so the torque reverses and the motor rotates in the opposite direction. Reversing both current and field together would preserve the original torque direction.

options.text: The soft-iron core becomes permanently magnetised and holds the armature.
The circuit remains closed because the hammer has not yet struck the bell.
The circuit breaks, the electromagnet loses most of its magnetism, and the spring returns the armature to remake contact.
The current increases indefinitely until the battery is exhausted.

explanation: Movement of the armature breaks the contact and interrupts the current. The electromagnet loses its magnetism, allowing the spring to return the armature and restore contact. This repeated make-and-break cycle produces the ringing sound.

question: The North pole of a bar magnet moves towards the left face of a stationary coil connected to a sensitive galvanometer. The coil's left face is initially not magnetised. Which statement correctly predicts the observation?

options.text: The galvanometer deflects while the magnet approaches; the induced current's direction opposes the change producing it.
The galvanometer remains at zero because only the coil is allowed to move in induction experiments.
The galvanometer deflects permanently even after the magnet stops.
The galvanometer deflects because the magnet transfers its permanent magnetism directly to the coil.

explanation: Relative motion changes the magnetic field linking the coil, inducing an emf and, in a closed circuit, a current. By Lenz's law, the induced effect opposes the change causing it. Once the magnet stops relative to the coil, the induced emf becomes zero.

options.text: It has the same direction because the North pole still faces the coil.
No current is induced because the magnet is moving away from the coil.
It has the same direction but a smaller magnitude because the magnet is farther away.

title: AC generator: Identifying the correct connections
question: A rectangular coil rotates between the North and South poles of a magnet. The two ends of the coil connect to two separate continuous slip rings mounted on the rotating shaft. Stationary carbon brushes touch the rings and connect to an external load. Why does this arrangement produce alternating current in the external circuit?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 220" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="42" width="43" height="100" rx="3" fill="#dc2626" /><rect x="285" y="42" width="43" height="100" rx="3" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="33" y="96" font-size="21" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">N</text><text x="306" y="96" font-size="21" fill="white" text-anchor="middle">S</text><rect x="80" y="60" width="180" height="65" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M170 125 L170 158" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" /><ellipse cx="154" cy="164" rx="8" ry="19" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><ellipse cx="186" cy="164" rx="8" ry="19" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="4" /><rect x="136" y="157" width="8" height="19" fill="#64748b" /><rect x="196" y="157" width="8" height="19" fill="#64748b" /><path d="M140 176 L140 195 L102 195 M200 176 L200 195 L238 195" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="95" y="190" width="14" height="10" fill="#64748b" /><rect x="231" y="190" width="14" height="10" fill="#64748b" /><text x="170" y="23" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Rotating armature coil</text><text x="170" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Two slip rings and stationary brushes</text></svg>

options.text: The brushes reverse their positions after each half-turn.
The slip rings maintain continuous contact while the rotating coil's induced emf reverses every half-turn.
The slip rings reverse the magnet's polarity every half-turn.
The slip rings convert the induced AC into unidirectional DC.

explanation: As the coil rotates, its sides exchange their motion relative to the magnetic field every half-turn. The induced emf reverses. Slip rings preserve the individual coil-end connections to the external circuit, allowing alternating current to flow. A split-ring commutator is used to obtain unidirectional output in a simple DC generator.

The graph below shows the idealised output voltage. Idealised full-wave, unidirectional pulsating output. Which statement is correct about the role of the split-ring commutator?

It makes the output perfectly constant and ripple-free.
It reverses the external connections every half-turn so that the external output remains in one direction, though its magnitude varies.
It makes the generator work without relative motion between the coil and magnetic field.

explanation: The induced emf within the rotating coil reverses every half-turn. The split-ring commutator simultaneously reverses the coil's connections to the external circuit, giving a unidirectional pulsating output. It does not produce perfectly steady DC.

title: AC generator: Maximum and zero induced emf
question: A rectangular coil rotates uniformly in a uniform magnetic field directed from left to right. Position P shows the plane of the coil perpendicular to the magnetic field; position Q shows the plane of the coil parallel to the field. At which positions is the magnitude of the induced emf maximum and zero, respectively, in an ideal generator rotating at constant speed?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 120" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 30 L128 30 M8 52 L128 52 M8 74 L128 74" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M39 25 L49 30 L39 35 M79 47 L89 52 L79 57 M99 69 L109 74 L99 79" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><rect x="61" y="18" width="18" height="70" fill="none" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="3" /><text x="70" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P: plane ⟂ B</text></svg>

options.text: Maximum at P; zero at Q.
Zero at P; maximum at Q.
Maximum at both P and Q.
Zero at both P and Q.

explanation: At P, the magnetic flux through the coil is at an extreme value, so its instantaneous rate of change is zero and the induced emf is zero. At Q, the flux is momentarily zero but changes most rapidly, so the induced emf is maximum. Confusing maximum flux with maximum emf is the key trap.

For an ideal transformer,


(V_s / V_p)=(N_s / N_p)
=(300 / 1200)=frac14


Therefore, V_s=240×frac14=60 V. Since the secondary voltage is lower than the primary voltage, the transformer is step-down.
